Europe, not present at this summit, is in the crosshairs of all three leaders. Trump remains in open dispute with European leaders over their dependency on US defence and alleged cultural decline. China is unhappy about the tariffs the EU is now considering, targeting its exports. And Russia is of course probing European unity over Ukraine. 

European leaders, including the UK, need to look hard at this trio and work out their response on security and trade. They have every incentive to work out a common front: a live war is taking place on their eastern flank, as their main security guarantor becomes increasingly unpredictable. And technological competition from China threatens to annihilate their manufacturing industries. 

Other countries will look at the same photograph and similarly count their friends and new alliances. The smaller the country, the more it needs the rule of international law and respect for international institutions. 

Xi, Trump and Putin may gather believing they dominate the world. But their meeting gives others every reason to look for ways to stand together.

item.title: Tom Friedman’s deceptive effort to lure Dems to escalate in Iran
item.description:
The centrist Democrats’ campaign to rescue - not end - Donald Trump’s illegal war with Iran has officially begun. Behold Tom Friedman’s column today in The New York Times.

Tom puts forward an argument with a clever structure. He starts by blasting Trump’s decision to start the war. He cites numerous data points, including testimony from GCC officials that tears massive holes in the White House’s narrative that the situation is under control, that Iran is on the ropes, and that Trump has won the battle for the Strait of Hormuz.

This paragraph, for instance:

“I had a briefing from a senior Emirati oil official who shared with me a digital map of the relentless Iranian attacks on the fleet of Emirati-owned oil tankers — not when they pass through the Strait of Hormuz near Iran, but when they try to transit the Persian Gulf in Emirati waters, hugging the country’s eastern coastline. These are highly sophisticated attacks, mostly with cruise missiles and drones, that go right into the oil tankers’ engine rooms and disable them. Bull’s-eye every time. The Emirates then has to send tugboats out to rescue the crews and pull the disabled tankers into port. This is happening almost every day.”

Now add the testimony from the head of the U.S. Navy, who revealed that insuring ships through the Strait of Hormuz has skyrocketed from $54,000 to a staggering $64 million. That’s a jaw-dropping 118,418 percent increase, a devastating indictment of just how unsustainable and ruinous Trump’s so-called control over the Strait has become. Having brought readers along with him, particularly centrist Democratic leaders in Congress whom this piece specifically targets, Tom takes a dark and sudden turn.

Rather than urging Democrats to help end the war, he pivots to arguing against cutting its funding, relying on arguments so flimsy and absurd they almost defy belief. Take this paragraph, for example:

“I think it would be a mistake for Democrats to try to cut off funding for the war, just as I thought it was a mistake to talk about defunding the police. You defund it, you own it. That is, Trump will say forevermore that he had the Iranians on the ropes and then the Democrats pulled the rug out from under him. Democrats should do nothing to weaken U.S. leverage on the Iranians. It is a sick regime and a truly destabilizing, malign actor in the region and around the world, one that is now providing Russians with the advanced drone technology that Moscow is using to destroy Ukraine’s energy infrastructure before winter.”

So in Tom’s upside-down logic, if Democrats defund the war, they own it, but if they keep funding it, somehow Trump still owns it. Reality, of course, is the reverse. If Democrats choose to bankroll an illegal war their voters have demanded they end, they become complicit, sharing the dubious distinction of co-ownership with Trump and Israel. As I’ve pointed out on this Substack, with shifting voting patterns—especially among younger voters—Democrats are setting themselves up for a reckoning in 2028 if they rescue the war instead of ending it.

This is a stunningly moronic argument Tom puts forward, but admittedly, it will resonate with centrist Democrats who have secretly supported the war all along.

Tom is correct, however, that Trump will falsely claim that he was about to win the war but that the Democrats “pulled the rug out from under him,” to which I respond: Who cares??

Should Democrats really keep an illegal, losing war alive just to stop Trump from spinning another feeble lie? Is this the leadership voters crave—turning a blind eye to an illegal war and the affordability crisis it fuels, all to obsess over Trump’s endless lying?

The American people can endure Trump’s lies. We live with them every day. What Americans cannot live with is a war that makes actual living an increasingly difficult proposition. A war that weakens the US on every front and that destabilizes the global economy to the point of a potential depression. But Tom believes Democrats should be more concerned about Trump adding one more lie to his repertoire.

Then Tom adds the ever-present false-choice argument that Washington’s foreign policy establishment obsesses over: If you do X, enemy Y will become stronger.

So defunding the war will make Iran stronger, Tom says, even though he admits that it is the war itself that has put Iran in a stronger position. So the Democrats should continue a losing war out of fear that ending the war will make the US lose even further. The Israeli officials who pushed Trump into this war in the first place could not have put it better.

But this sentence reveals the logical conclusion of Tom’s argument. In reality, he is not arguing for a mere continuation of the war. He wants the Democrats to escalate the war. Because, according to Tom’s own assessment, continuing the war will not change the picture: The US will lose more, regional countries will pay a high price, and Iran’s position will be strengthened.

The only way to reverse Iran’s gains, the implicit logic reads, is to escalate the war in order to press Iran back. This is the option the Israelis are pushing for. This is the option Trump is considering.

And this is the option Tom is deceptively luring Democrats into enabling.

item.title: The Guardian view on the Trump, Xi and Putin meeting: it may be a first, but it’s not progress | Editorial
item.description:
A trilateral gathering is good news for China and Russia, but bad for the US – and its traditional allies

“Historic” is a neutral descriptor, not a favourable one. Things can be unprecedented for good reason. Donald Trump’s meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China on Thursday will be the first time that the leaders of the US, China and Russia have gathered for talks as a trio. The trilateral on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is striking, but it is not an achievement.

The lack of a clear agenda is telling: the spectacle really is the substance. Mr Trump sees international affairs in terms of spheres of influence. This meeting reinforces the obvious conclusion for the rest of the world – that they don’t get to sit at the table, only to be on the plate. Mr Xi promotes the notion of a multipolar world. Others would be more sympathetic if all three governments were not determinedly undermining multilateralism.

Bahrain runs into the buzzsaw of US war, reacts predictably
item.description:
On Monday, the High Criminal Court in Bahrain’s capital, Manama, sentenced dozens of Shiite clerics to life in prison, on allegations that they “communicated with..and had collected and received funds” from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

As the trial was running its course, Iranian drones were targeting U.S. military installations in Bahrain, with attacks taking place on Friday, Sunday, and again on Tuesday and Wednesday, ending a two-month lull.

Bahrain, the small island kingdom on the eastern side of the Arabian Peninsula, is where the pressures of the U.S.-Iran war are concentrated most tightly. A majority Shia population run by a Sunni ruling family, Bahrain has a current population of 1.6 million people (fewer than half, about 740,000 are citizens; the rest are largely migrant workers, mainly from South Asia) and is home to the U.S. Navy’s Fifth Fleet. It signed the Abraham Accords with Israel, and is also a deeply indebted nation, dependent on its wealthier neighbors for its survival.

This is a volatile mix, and Washington has spent the last nine months, through its war on Iran, piling the pressure on its most vulnerable ally in the region.

Bahrain was ruled from the Persian side of the Gulf for long stretches of its history until 1783, when the Al Khalifa, a Sunni Arab clan from what is today Qatar, took the island and expelled the Iranian-installed governor. Their descendants now form the royal family that rules Bahrain.

Iran, however, never quite accepted this arrangement. Its parliament declared Bahrain the country’s fourteenth province in 1957, and only in 1970, after a U.N. survey found Bahrainis overwhelmingly wanted independence, did the Shah of Iran drop the claim.

The Islamic Republic that now governs Iran has not entirely let go of the past. In April, Kayhan, the Tehran daily whose editor was appointed by the late supreme leader, ran a column declaring that “Bahrain was and is part of Iranian territory.” Hossein Shariatmadari, Kayhan’s managing editor, went on to characterize the ruling family as “puppets of the British government” and accused Bahrain of direct participation in American military attacks on Iran.

The last claim reflects the official government line: Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei defended Iran’s attacks on Bahrain this week, claiming that countries in the region aided American forces, and that Tehran’s strikes were “purely defensive in nature.”

While annexation of Bahrain is not Iranian policy, irredentist rhetoric from hardliners in Tehran has become useful to Bahrain’s leadership, who leverage these threats to frame dissident citizens as a potential fifth column.

As Bahrain’s demographics make clear, it is structurally distinct from its oil-rich, Sunni majority Arab Gulf neighbors. It ran out of meaningful oil reserves long ago and never had the revenue to buy the loyalty of its population. Instead, what it has done is direct a large share of state employment and patronage to its Sunni tribal base, while its Shiite citizens, who make up 55 to 62 percent of the population, are largely excluded from the military and security apparatus where the overwhelming majority of officers are Sunni (many are naturalized foreign-born recruits), and live in underserved neighborhoods and villages.

The fear of Iran is the glue that holds this system together, and that fear is not totally imagined. Bahrain’s government said it foiled a coup attempt in 1981 by a Tehran-linked group known as the Islamic Front for the Liberation of Bahrain. Grand Ayatollah Isa Qassim, the kingdom's most senior Shiite cleric, who was stripped of Bahraini nationality in 2016 and sentenced to life imprisonment in absentia on Monday, has lived in Iran since 2018. Manama also accuses other exiles living there of directing armed attacks on Bahraini police.

But the same fear has also become a convenient justification for Bahrain’s rulers to treat nearly all dissent, including through peaceful means, as treasonous and Iran-backed. This is what happened in 2011, when the Arab Spring came to Bahrain, and a protest movement that included both sects was crushed with the help of Saudi and Emirati troops. Bahrain’s King Hamad used the episode to hint at Iranian involvement.

The same is happening again now. Since the U.S. and Israel initiated hostilities against Iran on February 28, Tehran has retaliated against every Gulf state hosting American forces. Bahrain has, as a result, absorbed hundreds of missiles and drones, which not only struck the Navy’s Fifth Fleet headquarters, but also industrial and residential sites, and a desalination plant.

What made Bahrain’s leadership especially nervous was how some Bahrainis publicly mourned Iran’s slain supreme leader Ali Khamenei, who was killed in the opening blows of the war.

What followed was a crackdown that swept more than 700 people, for filming attacks, and for social media activity deemed anti-government or pro-Iran. In April, the government stripped 69 citizens of their nationality for “glorifying or sympathising with the hostile Iranian acts” and postponed parliamentary elections.

In May and June, Bahraini authorities arrested more than 50 clerics, whose sentences were handed down on Monday.

Within the first 24 hours of that verdict, Iran’s foreign ministry and Qais al-Khazali, the leader of an Iran-backed Iraqi militia, issued statements assailing the trials and sentences. In rushing to defend Bahraini clerics, Iran and its allies hand Manama what looks to it like proof that the convicted answer to foreign patrons, which then fuels harsher repressive measures, and so the cycle continues.

The economic picture for Manama is also dire. Before the war, the International Monetary Fund had put Bahrain's government debt at 134 percent of GDP, among the highest in the world. It is also the only Gulf Cooperative Council state rated “junk” by all three credit agencies, meaning investors view its bonds as high-risk and demand high interest rates to lend its government money. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz by Iran has cut off nearly all of its modest oil exports and forced its aluminum smelter, the Gulf’s largest, to declare force majeure.

Bahrain has been bailed out before, by Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Kuwait to the tune of $10 billion in 2018. It will likely be bailed out again, but this time, its primary donor is strained. Saudi Arabia is fighting its own war with the Houthis in Yemen who have hit Riyadh’s airport and business center, and its critical East-West pipeline, which moves roughly four million barrels of crude per day from the Gulf to the Red Sea.

Riyadh is also running a deficit currently projected at $65 billion dollars, up from the $44 billion planned in January, which makes the contours of any future bailout hard to predict.

Whatever form that rescue takes, it will certainly come with strings. Given Bahrain's size and its modest economic means, its freedom of action is limited and it has typically followed the lead of its larger neighbors when it comes to foreign policy.

Before the war, Bahrain was pursuing rapprochement with the Islamic Republic. Despite being one of the inaugural signers of the Abraham Accords with Israel in 2020, it reopened channels with Tehran in 2024, prompted in part by the Saudi-Iranian détente that China brokered in 2023. The current war sealed that opening shut, and now Manama has little room to negotiate with Iran on its own until a wider settlement is worked out.

Yet rather than holding out for diplomacy, Bahrain has taken a more assertive line, using its seat as a non-permanent member of the U.N. Security Council to push resolutions demanding Iran reopen the Strait and stop its attacks on its neighbors. One was adopted in March and later one, which initially contained language authorizing the use of force, was vetoed by Russia and China, who argued it was one-sided for ignoring U.S. and Israeli strikes that provoked Iran’s reaction.

These moves are unlikely to have endeared the kingdom to Tehran, and may also help in understanding why Bahrain has remained in Iran’s crosshairs.

item.title: Trump’s honeymoon with South Korea is over
item.description:
Following his visit to the White House to meet with President Donald Trump in August of last year, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung had good reasons to believe the strategic alliance was in strong shape.

Despite their ideological disagreements, the two leaders held a cordial first summit that in subsequent months led to a resolution of their trade frictions, a $150 billion investment in shipbuilding, substantial investment in commercial projects in the United States, and even a surprise announcement that Trump would help Seoul build nuclear-powered submarines. One of Lee’s key commitments was to increase South Korean defense spending to 3.5% of GDP — the Trump administration’s minimum target for Asian nations.

But what a difference a year can make with Trump. On October 21, U.S. Ambassador to South Korea Michelle Steel publicly described the relationship as experiencing “turbulence.” Lee’s government, for its part, has tried to downplay recent tensions, arguing that overheated domestic politics in both countries need not undermine the strong foundation of the alliance. As South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun told Parliament in late October, “When you’re in turbulence, fasten your seat belt and it won’t be a problem.”

In truth, some of the turbulence is of Seoul’s own making. In March, for example, South Korean Unification Minister Chung Dong-young publicly identified a North Korean uranium enrichment facility, potentially compromising sensitive sources and methods. The Lee government insists that the information was already public, but Washington disagrees and has retaliated by restricting certain satellite-derived intelligence about North Korea and excluded Seoul from a trilateral meeting on North Korean cyber threats.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio has complained about intelligence sharing broadly with Seoul, and South Korean Ambassador Kang Kyung-wha acknowledged as recently as last month that his government had not fully addressed Washington’s concerns.

South Korea has also been slow in deciding how to invest its pledged $350 billion, angering Trump in the process. For instance, Trump wants Seoul to invest roughly $54 billion in the Alaska LNG pipeline project, but Lee’s government has questioned its commercial viability. Although he has expressed confidence that South Korea will eventually follow through, Trump has made vague threats to resume tariffs if the deals remain stalled.

Separately, South Korean regulators imposed a fine of $423 million on Coupang, a U.S.-listed e-commerce company, following a massive consumer data breach. The Trump administration and congressional Republicans were outraged by the move, calling it discrimination against American companies, while the Lee administration justified the measure to protect consumer privacy data.

But the Trump administration shares much of the blame for the increasingly contentious bilateral relationship. For one thing, even though Washington and Seoul already agreed in June 2025 to reduce tariffs from 25% to 15% in 2025, Trump periodically threatens to raise tariff rates again to 25% when he gets angry about something. This has surprised and frustrated South Korean officials, who may no longer see Washington as a reliable strategic ally. And perhaps neither do the South Korean people. According to a Pew Research survey from August, 55% of them hold an unfavorable view of the United States — the highest such mark in more than 20 years.

North Korea poses a bilateral challenge as well. To be sure, both Trump and Lee want to prioritize renewed engagement with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un rather than deterrence. But the Trump administration’s preferred approach differs from Seoul’s. Trump surprised South Korea by shortening the annual bilateral military drills, known as Ulchi Freedom Guardian, just hours before they began. He argued that they were unnecessarily provocative toward Kim, whom Trump hopes will join him in a summit.

Although he publicly accepted Trump’s decision to cut back combined military exercises, Lee would rather derive diplomatic leverage from enhanced military preparedness against North Korea, and the deterrence that comes with it, prior to negotiations. Trump further blamed South Korea for not contributing to the U.S. naval operation to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, in turn questioning why Washington continues to defend South Korea on the peninsula.

Deepening disagreements over China represent yet another irritant. The Trump administration clearly seeks greater “flexibility” in how it uses the approximately 28,500 U.S. troops deployed to South Korea. Rather than focusing exclusively on North Korea, Washington has publicly intimated that China could be the target of their future military operations, and that Seoul would be expected to support that mission.

Undersecretary of Defense Elbridge “Bridge” Colby, for example, visited Seoul in January and gave a speech at the Sejong Institute that curiously did not mention North Korea at all, and instead, replaced it with multiple references to countering China. To the shock of South Korean officials, Trump’s National Security Strategy, released last November, neglected to mention North Korea either and focused instead on the need for South Korea to help the U.S. and Japan secure the First Island Chain — a clear reference to containing China. Although Trump’s National Defense Strategy from January did reference North Korea, it avoided stating that denuclearization was still a U.S. priority and put the responsibility to deal with the regime more squarely on Seoul, with limited American support.

Trump’s submarine and shipbuilding deals are also in limbo. On the submarines, Trump wants them built at the South Korean defense firm Hanwha’s shipyard in Philadelphia, but the Lee government argues that South Korea offers more appropriate shipyards because they are already outfitted with advanced submarine-building capabilities. There is also the question surrounding the enriched nuclear fuel and associated sensitive technologies, which Seoul wants Washington to provide. But rules governing the bilateral relationship currently do not permit such transfers without specific exemptions or additional authorizations.

When the submarine deal was first announced in October 2025, none of these issues had been properly considered by the Trump administration, provoking the current disputes. And on broader shipbuilding, South Korea’s $150 billion financial commitment has largely stalled. Indeed, the president’s Make American Shipbuilding Great Again (MASGA) initiative has yielded zero concrete projects, embarrassing Trump, who wants to reenergize the U.S. defense industrial base and add manufacturing jobs. Progress on MASGA has also been hampered by a mix of legal, political, and financial obstacles.

Finally, the fallout from the September 2025 ICE raids on South Korean workers at the Hyundai-LG battery plant in the United States continues. Although Seoul wrapped up its internal investigation without retaliating against the U.S. government, attorneys representing more than 300 of the workers, who were allegedly shackled and abused during the ordeal, are now pursuing administrative damages, possibly a precursor to civil lawsuits, against the Department of Justice, the Department of Homeland Security, the FBI, and others. The political rhetoric surrounding the case became heated on both sides as the legal process continues to unfold.

Despite the growing tensions between them, South Korea and the U.S. remain staunch allies, and in fact, the Trump administration has referred to Seoul as a “model ally,” especially because of its increased defense spending. Lee and Trump reportedly spoke about future diplomatic engagements on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China this week. But difficulties remain, and the next two years under Trump and Lee could prove even more turbulent when it comes to trade, investment, military cooperation, and foreign policy.

Additionally, while many have interpreted the midterm elections as a rebuke of Trump’s foreign policy, they are unlikely to affect U.S.-Korea relations in substantive ways. The president typically has the lead on foreign policy, and lame-duck presidents tend to intensify their focus on it to secure their legacy. For South Korea, this likely means more, not less, of Trump, adding to Seoul’s urgency to somehow figure him out and stop making unforced errors.

item.description:
Nvidia’s former CEO, Jensen Huang, and his extramarital relationship with the alleged Chinese agent Alice Huang, likely will be discussed at the scheduled meeting of President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the 2026 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen, China on November 18-19.

It is alleged that Ms. Huang, Managing Director of MegaSpeed International in Singapore and a cloud partner with Nvidia in the Asia-Pacific region, was an agent of China’s Ministry of State Security. She allegedly was part of a “honey trap” operation against Jensen Huang. It is alleged that her company, MegaSpeed , purchased billions of dollars of advanced Artificial Intelligence (AI) chips and servers, and in violation of U.S. export-control restrictions, smuggled these advanced AI chips to China.

A spokesperson at China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the allegation that Ms. Huang was a Chinese agent is “baseless” and “slanderous”.

Mr. Trump reportedly said he will not address this issue in his meeting with Mr. Xi, although it is likely that Mr. Xi will address these allegations. Neither the U.S. nor Singapore has filed criminal charges against Ms. Huang, and the Department of Justice said it is looking into the matter without reaching any formal conclusions. It is likely that Congress will conduct hearings related to these allegations.

Both leaders are scheduled to will meet on the margins of the APEC Leaders’ meeting. Russia’s President Vladimir Putin will also attend the APEC session and meet with Presidents Trump and Xi – the first-ever trilateral meeting on the sideline of APEC.

This will be third meeting of Presidents Trump and Xi this year, with a fourth meeting scheduled for December 14 to 15, 2026, at the G20 Leaders’ Summit in Miami, Florida.

Although a formal agenda for the trilateral meeting has not been published, it is likely the three leaders will discuss the wars in Ukraine and Iran, with some discussion of North Korea and its nuclear and missile programs. Both China and Russia have a close allied relationship with Pyongyang. They can – if they want – use their relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un to attempt to convince him to meet for a fourth time with Mr. Trump.

Working-level teams from the three countries reportedly have been negotiating an agenda covering AI in critical weapons systems and a potential joint statement against nuclear war.

Nuclear proliferation is another subject the three leaders will discuss, with the U.S. continuing to encourage China to agree to greater transparency on their nuclear program and an eventual arms control agreement. Previously, China refused to discuss their nuclear program, noting that the U.S. and Russia had significantly more nuclear warheads than China. Once parity in the number of nuclear warheads is reached, China said they would then consider discussing their nuclear program with the U.S.

At the APEC conference, AI and the Digital Economies will be discussed, with emphasis on narrowing the regional digital divide and discussing cross-border digital trade interoperability. Work force reskilling and aligning AI with the energy infrastructure were subjects previously discussed at APEC Ministerial talks.

And given global economic fragmentation and rising costs, officials will prioritize cross-border supply chain stability and interoperability across different national regulatory systems. China is also highlighting regional connectivity through the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao greater bay area initiative.

The APEC meeting will also discuss the green-digital transition, clean energy, food security, and ocean and fisheries sustainability in the Asia-Pacific region.

Regional trade and economic integration will also be discussed, given that 2026 marks the 20th anniversary of the Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific vision, that focused on multilateral trade and reducing tariffs.

This APEC meeting will be impactful, given the participation of Presidents Trump, Xi, and Putin.

item.title: Riyadh’s tallest skyscraper hit in Houthi strike on Saudi wealth fund HQ
item.description:
By Timour Azhari

RIYADH, Nov 19 (Reuters) - Riyadh's tallest skyscraper, headquarters of the Saudi sovereign wealth fund, was struck on Thursday by a suspected Houthi missile in the latest blow in the Iran-backed Yemeni group's war with the kingdom.

The strike blew out windows across seven to eight floors of PIF Tower, bending parts of its metal facade. It was the second time in less than two weeks that a Houthi attack damaged a landmark in Riyadh's financial district, with state oil giant Aramco's building hit in a November 8 attack.

item.title: Trump says US will 'see what happens' in conflict with Iran after January 1
item.description:
Nov 19 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump said in comments broadcast on Thursday that the United States would "see what happens" in its conflict with Iran after January 1, without explaining what the significance of that date might be.

In recent weeks, Trump has alternated between threats of escalation against Iran and indicating he could wind down hostilities, with the two sides in a standoff over efforts to resolve the conflict.

item.title: West presses Iran at IAEA to let inspections resume at bombed nuclear sites
item.description:
By Francois Murphy

VIENNA, Nov 19 (Reuters) - The United States, Britain, France and Germany jointly pressed Tehran at a meeting of the UN atomic watchdog's board on Thursday to let inspectors return to its nuclear sites bombed by the US and Israel last year, accusing Tehran of "stonewalling".

Iran has not granted the International Atomic Energy Agency access to those nuclear facilities since the military strikes against them in June 2025.

item.title: Iraqi forces strike compromise with powerful pro-Iran militia, security officials say
item.description:
By Ahmed Rasheed

BAGHDAD, Nov 19 (Reuters) - Iraq has reached a compromise with the powerful Iran-backed militia Kataib Hezbollah, three senior security officials said, after Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi readied security forces to move against the group.

Iraqi officials had accused the group of running a smuggling ring that siphoned off hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of state-owned oil.

item.title: World court finds Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya population
item.description:
THE HAGUE, Nov 19 (Reuters) - The World Court on Thursday ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Muslim minority Rohingya population.

It is the first time a state has been found responsible for genocide at the court.

The ruling marked only the fourth time since the Nazi Holocaust that an international court ruled that the crime had been committed.

(Reporting by Stephanie van den Berg and Anthony Deutsch, editing by Bart Meijer)

item.title: Israel says it concludes Gaza tank raid
item.description:
By Nidal al-Mughrabi

CAIRO, Nov 19 (Reuters) - Israel’s military said on Thursday it had concluded a tank raid to dismantle a suspected Hamas tunnel in the central Gaza Strip, its highest-profile ground incursion across the yellow ceasefire line since a truce halted major fighting more than a year ago.

Posting a message to the people of Gaza on Facebook, the military said its forces ended an "activity against Hamas infrastructure" in the area, and that the main north-south Salahudeen road had been reopened for traffic.

item.title: World Court finds Myanmar forces killed thousands of Rohingya, ruling ongoing
item.description:
THE HAGUE, Nov 19 (Reuters) - Myanmar's security forces killed thousands of members of the Rohingya minority Muslim population and committed widespread sexual violence, judges at the World Court ruled on Thursday.

A reading of the verdict was ongoing.

"The Court finds that Myanmar's security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence as well as acts of extreme violence against children and attacked fleeing Rohingya as they sought to flee in large numbers to Bangladesh," the court said.

item.title: Trump says Board of Trade has brought 'greater balance' to US-China ties
item.description:
By Jarrett Renshaw and Kanishka Singh

SHENZHEN, China/WASHINGTON, Nov 19 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that the Board of ​Trade that he and Chinese ⁠President Xi Jinping ​agreed to form ​at their summit in Beijing in May had brought "greater balance to a very lopsided relationship" between the two countries.

Trump made his comments at the start of a meeting with Xi during the APEC summit in China and said the US and China had split their tariffs in a fair way.

item.title: China and Russia release 'peace declaration' after Trump, Xi, Putin meeting
item.description:
By Jarrett Renshaw and Trevor Hunnicutt

SHENZHEN, China, Nov 19 (Reuters) - Chinese President Xi Jinping and his US and Russian counterparts Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin agreed on a "peace declaration" at their unprecedented three-way meeting on Thursday in which they reaffirmed that a nuclear war should never be fought, China and Russia said.

The declaration capped Trump's three-day diplomatic swing through Asia that produced few tangible victories, despite his repeated boasts about making history and brokering peace.

item.title: China, US, Russia issue 'peace declaration' after first summit
item.description:
China, the United States and Russia issued a "peace declaration" Thursday following an unprecedented leaders' summit, almost five years into the Ukraine war and with Donald Trump bogged down in Iran.

The statement after Xi Jinping, Trump and Vladimir Putin met in China, said that they wanted to reform the United Nations, to protect diplomatic immunity and boost supply and production of refined petroleum products.
